tips.title: Four papers, a quarter each
tips.body: Speaking, Listening, Reading and Writing are **25% each** and **50 marks each** — 200 marks in all. No paper counts for more than another, so the one you like least is worth exactly as much as the one you like best.

tips.title: Answer in English where the question is in English
tips.body: In **Listening Section A** and the whole **Reading** paper the questions are set in English and answered in English. A beautiful French answer there scores **nothing**. Check the language of the question before you write a word.

tips.title: Translation into English needs every word
tips.body: In Reading you translate a French passage into English. **Every word and every tense has to be accounted for** — a phrase left out loses its mark even if the rest is perfect. Translate it all, then read your English back to check it sounds natural.

tips.title: The dictation is heard three times
tips.body: Listening Section B plays each sentence **3 times**: use the first to hear the whole sentence, the second to fill the gaps, the third to check spelling, accents and silent endings. Knowing the pattern in advance is half the technique.

tips.title: Fifteen minutes to prepare the speaking
tips.body: Speaking gives you **15 minutes** of preparation — 14 in the invigilation room and **1 in the exam room to say the read aloud out loud**. That last minute is the only chance to hear the hard words before they count, so use it.

steps.title: Les quatre épreuves
steps.body:
GCSE French is **four papers**, each worth **50 marks** and **25%** of the grade — 200 marks and 227 minutes in total at Higher tier.

**Paper 1 — Speaking** (27 minutes with the preparation). Three tasks in a fixed order: a **read aloud** with a short interaction after it, a **role play**, and a **picture task**. At Higher tier the read aloud alone carries **12 of the 50 marks**, leaving 38 for the other two.

**Paper 2 — Listening** (60 minutes, including 5 minutes' reading time). **Section A** is comprehension: questions in English, answers in English. **Section B** is a **dictation**: short French sentences, each heard 3 times, written down in French.

**Paper 3 — Reading** (60 minutes). Questions in English, answers in English, plus a **passage to translate from French into English**.

**Paper 4 — Writing** (80 minutes). Written **in French throughout**, including an extended response of around **80 to 90 words**.

The four **assessment objectives** match the four papers exactly — listening, speaking, reading and writing, 25% each — so there is no paper to neglect.

steps.title: Répondre en anglais
steps.body:
The commonest avoidable loss of marks in GCSE French is answering in **the wrong language**.

**Listening Section A and the whole Reading paper** set their questions **in English** and expect answers **in English**. An answer written in French scores nothing there, however good the French is. Before you write, look at the language of the question.

**Paper 4 Writing and Paper 1 Speaking** are the opposite: **French throughout**.

**Answering comprehension questions well**:

- Give **exactly what is asked** — if the question asks for one reason, one reason is enough; a list risks contradicting itself.
- Include the **detail**: a time, a number, a reason, a negative. *He does not play football* is a different answer from *he plays football*.
- Watch the **negatives**: *ne … pas, ne … jamais, ne … plus* reverse a sentence, and a listener hunting for familiar nouns misses them.
- Watch the **tense**: *j'ai joué* (did), *je joue* (does), *je vais jouer* (will) are three different answers.

**Don't translate the whole text.** Comprehension marks come from finding the answer, not from rendering every sentence. Save full translation for the question that actually asks for it.

steps.title: Translation into English
steps.body: The Reading paper ends with a French passage to turn into English. The method is to account for every word first, then make the English natural.

visuals.problem: Translate: « Quand j'étais petite, je n'aimais pas le collège. Maintenant j'y vais avec plaisir, parce que j'ai de meilleures notes. J'apprends le français depuis cinq ans. »

steps.text: *Quand j'étais petite* → **When I was little** — imperfect, and *petite* shows a female speaker.
*je n'aimais pas le collège* → **I did not like school** — the negative must survive the translation.
*Maintenant j'y vais avec plaisir* → **Now I go there happily** — *y* is *there*, and must be translated.
steps.note: a small word still carries a mark

steps.text: *parce que j'ai de meilleures notes* → **because I get better marks** — *meilleures* is *better*, not *more good*.
*J'apprends le français depuis cinq ans* → **I have been learning French for five years** — present + *depuis* becomes an English perfect.
steps.note: the tense changes shape in English

steps.title: Le speaking et la dictée
steps.body:
**Paper 1 has three tasks, always in this order.**

**1. Read aloud** — a short French text read out, then a short interaction. Worth **12 of 50** marks at Higher. Read French *as French*: leave the silent endings silent (*ils jouent* sounds like *ils joue*), make the liaisons (*les_enfants*), keep the nasal vowels (*on, en, un*), and use the text's own punctuation for phrasing.

**2. Role play** — you play a part in a set situation and respond in French to each prompt. **Every prompt must be covered**; one skipped prompt is marks gone. One prompt is always *ask a question*, so have *À quelle heure… ? C'est combien ? Est-ce que vous avez… ?* ready.

**3. Picture task** — describe a photo, then answer questions that widen out into the topic. The shape that scores is **describe, then give an opinion, then bring in a second tense**: *Sur la photo, il y a… · À mon avis, c'est… parce que… · Moi, l'année dernière, j'ai…*

**Preparation**: 15 minutes — 14 in the invigilation room, then **1 minute in the exam room to practise the read aloud out loud**.

**The dictation** (Listening Section B): French sentences written down in French, each heard **3 times**. Spelling, accents and **silent endings** all count — the *-ent* you never hear, the agreement you cannot hear, the final consonant that stays silent but must be written.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Name the four papers and say what each is worth.
2. Which parts of the exam are answered in English?
3. How many times is each dictation sentence played?

**Part B.**

4. Translate into English: *je ne vais jamais au cinéma*.
5. Write three questions you could use for the "ask a question" prompt in a role play.
6. Write the three-part shape of a good picture-task answer.

**Part C.**

7. Translate into English, accounting for every word: *quand j'étais petit, je n'avais pas de portable, mais maintenant j'en ai un*.
8. Write down what you would do with each of the three dictation hearings.
9. Plan a revision week: which paper you would work on each day, and how.

For question 7, check the tense and the negative both survive into your English.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Check the language of the question, every time.** English question, English answer. It costs nothing and it is the single biggest avoidable loss in the exam.

**Listen for the words that change the meaning.** *Ne … pas, ne … jamais, ne … plus*, and the tense markers *hier, demain, avant*. A candidate hunting for familiar nouns hears *foot* and *samedi* and writes the opposite of what was said.

**Account for every word in the translation.** Small words — *y, en, déjà, encore, ne … que* — each carry meaning. Translate them, then reread the English on its own and make it sound like English.

**Change the tense shape where English needs it.** *J'apprends le français depuis cinq ans* is *I **have been** learning*, not *I learn*. *Je jouais* is *I used to play* or *I was playing*. This is where the translation marks are won.

**Use the read aloud preparation minute.** Say the text out loud once, and pick out the words with silent endings, liaisons and nasal vowels before they count. 12 of 50 speaking marks sit in that one task.

**Cover every role-play prompt.** A prompt you skip is a mark you cannot get back, and the "ask a question" prompt is the one candidates most often forget.

**Build the picture task in three moves.** Describe, then an opinion with a reason, then a second tense. That order gives the examiner everything the mark scheme lists.

**Use all three dictation hearings differently.** Listening three times the same way wastes two of them.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Four papers**, 50 marks and **25%** each: Speaking, Listening, Reading, Writing — 200 marks in all.
- **Speaking** (27 min): read aloud (**12** marks), role play, picture task; **15 minutes** preparation, the last **1** in the exam room.
- **Listening** (60 min): Section A in English, Section B a **dictation** in French, each sentence heard **3** times.
- **Reading** (60 min): English questions and answers, plus a **translation into English**.
- **Writing** (80 min): **French throughout**, with an extended response of about **80 to 90 words**.
- **English question → English answer.** French there scores nothing.
- Give the **detail**: times, numbers, reasons, negatives.
- Watch *ne … pas / jamais / plus* and the tense markers.
- In translation, **account for every word**, then make the English natural.
- *Depuis* + present → *have been doing*; imperfect → *used to / was doing*.
- Role play: **cover every prompt**, including *ask a question*.
- Picture task: **describe · opinion with a reason · a second tense**.
- Dictation: whole sentence, then gaps, then check accents and silent endings.

examTechnique.body:
Four papers, **50 marks and 25% each**, so none can be neglected. **Check the language of the question**: English questions take English answers, and Writing and Speaking are French throughout.

In comprehension give the **detail** asked for and listen for the negatives and tense markers. In translation **account for every word**, then make the English natural. In speaking, cover **every** role-play prompt, build the picture task as *describe · opinion with a reason · a second tense*, and spend the exam-room minute saying the read aloud out loud.
examinerErrors: Answering in French where the question is in English.
Missing a negative and giving the opposite answer.
Leaving a word or phrase out of the translation.
Translating depuis + present as a simple present.
Skipping a role-play prompt, usually the question.
Describing a photo with no opinion or second tense.
Using all three dictation hearings in the same way.
Revising only the papers you enjoy.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 candidate checks the language of every question before writing, answers comprehension with exactly the detail asked for, and hears *ne … pas*, *jamais* and *plus* as the words that decide the answer. In translation every word is accounted for and the tenses are reshaped into natural English — *depuis* + present as *have been doing*, the imperfect as *used to*. In speaking, every role-play prompt is covered including the question, the picture task runs description, opinion with a reason, then a second tense, and the preparation minute is spent saying the read aloud out loud.
